title: dTBI: A paradigm for closed-head injury in Drosophila
protocol: Lay out the components on the lab bench, removing each component from their packaging.
Drill a small hole in the left side of the enclosure, towards the corner, approximately 10mm in diameter (~7/16”).
Push the female connector through the hole from the inside of the enclosure.
Tighten the nut to secure the connector to the enclosure.
Rotate the red button on the power supply with a flat bladed screwdriver to set the voltage output to 12V.
Connect the largest diameter plug (5.5mm) to the end of the black wire extending from the power supply.
Strip approximately ¼” of covering from each end of the black and red wires using wire strippers.
Attach male Dupont connectors to the metal pins of the red and black wires if soldering is not desired.
Solder a single header pin to each end of the red and black wires if soldering is preferred.
Position Breadboard #1 in the top left quadrant of the enclosure as shown in Fig 4, S1.
Align the red and blue lines labeled ‘+’ and ‘-’ vertically inside the enclosure.
Tack the bottom of the breadboard to the base of the enclosure using a hot glue gun.
Connect the pin from the red wire of the power supply to the left red column of the breadboard.
Connect the pin from the black wire of the power supply to the right blue column of the breadboard.
Use a multimeter and connect the probe tip from the ‘+’ terminal of the multimeter to the pin of the ‘+’ terminal of the power supply (red wire) on the breadboard.
While maintaining contact with the ‘+’ terminal, place the tip of the second probe from the multimeter (‘-’ or GND/COM connection) to the pin from the ‘-’ terminal (black wire) of the power supply.
Ask someone to assist and plug in the power supply, turning on the multimeter for a reading.
The multimeter should read ~12V on the display.
Disconnect the power supply.
Locate the blue potentiometer on the buck converter.
Identify the three pins connecting the potentiometer to the buck converter.
Turn on a soldering iron and wait until it reaches working temperature.
Touch the tip of the soldering iron to one exposed pin.
Melt the solder connecting the pin to the buck converter.
Remove the solder from each of the three pins of the potentiometer.
Carefully remove the potentiometer from the buck converter.
Place the buck converter in the enclosure, locating it in the bottom left quadrant.
Orient the buck converter so that +OUT and -OUT terminals point to the right.
Make a mark on the enclosure base to identify the location of the two mounting holes.
Remove the converter from the enclosure.
Drill pilot holes into the enclosure for mounting the buck converter.
Install nylon standoffs to mount the buck converter in the enclosure.
Cut and strip both ends of a green wire.
Solder one stripped end of the green wire to the middle terminal (C) of the new potentiometer.
Solder the remaining end of the green wire into the middle hole on the circuit board where the potentiometer was removed.
Cut and strip both ends of a red wire.
Solder one end of the red wire to one end terminal of the potentiometer.
Solder the remaining end of the red wire to one of the holes formerly holding the buck converter potentiometer.
Cut and strip both ends of a black wire.
Solder one end of the black wire to the third terminal of the potentiometer.
Solder the remaining end of the black wire to the last connection point for the potentiometer in the buck converter.
Cut and strip both ends of a red wire.
Solder one end of the red wire to the +IN terminal of the buck converter.
Connect the remaining end of the red wire to the +12V voltage rail on the breadboard.
Cut and strip both ends of a black wire.
Solder one end of the black wire to the -IN terminal of the buck converter.
Connect the remaining end of the black wire to the GND rail of the breadboard.
Orient the relay so the top right connects into position F10 on the breadboard.
Connect the lower left corner of the relay into position E12 on the breadboard.
Cut and strip a green wire, solder one end to +OUT on the buck converter.
Connect the other end of the green wire to position D10 on the breadboard.
Connect a new black wire from GND rail to position G13 on the breadboard.
Strip the ends of red, black, and white wires from the digital display.
Connect the red wire to +12V voltage rail of the breadboard.
Connect the black wire to the GND rail.
Connect the white wire into the breadboard at position C10.
Place the Arduino Microcontroller in the top right quadrant of the enclosure.
Position the USB connection towards the back wall of the enclosure and touch it to the wall.
Mark the four mounting holes for the Arduino on the enclosure base.
Remove the microcontroller, drill appropriate holes in the enclosure base.
Mark the opening needed for the USB connection (approximately 14mm x 14 mm).
Cut the opening for the USB connection.
Mount the Arduino using nylon standoffs.
Connect one end of a red wire to the Vin terminal on the Arduino and the other end to the +12V voltage rail of the breadboard.
Connect one end of a black wire to a GND terminal of the microcontroller and the other end to the GND rail of the breadboard.
Cut and strip a red wire, soldering one end into a post of the pushbutton switch.
Connect the remaining end of this red wire into the +5V terminal on the Arduino microcontroller.
Connect the remaining end of the red wire to pin #7 of the microcontroller.
Connect a new red wire from pin #13 of the Arduino microcontroller to position G10 of the breadboard (connecting to terminal #5 of the SPST relay).
Place Breadboard #2 in the bottom right quadrant of the enclosure.

Press the proportional voltage booster into the breadboard, positioning it to electrically isolate the INPUT and OUTPUT sides by connecting +INPUT to C12, -INPUT to C18, +OUTPUT to I20, and -OUTPUT to I10.
Connect one end of a green wire to the +INPUT terminal of the proportional voltage booster at position B12.
Connect the other end of the green wire to position D12 of Breadboard #1 (terminal #2 of the SPST relay).
Connect one end of a black wire from position B18 of Breadboard #2 (-INPUT of the proportional voltage booster) to the -OUT terminal of the buck converter.
Connect another end of a black wire from position A18 of Breadboard #2 (-INPUT of the booster) to the GND rail of Breadboard #1.
Cut and strip the ends from one half of the electrical terminal connector.
Solder header pins to each end of the wire if soldering is preferred, connecting the pin from the red wire to position I20.
Connect the pin from the black wire to position I10.
Drill a hole in the top of the enclosure to mount the potentiometer.
Drill a hole in the side for the electrical connector, tying a loop in the wiring to prevent it from pulling out.
Mount the digital display and pushbutton to the top of the enclosure.
Attach a USB cable to the Arduino microcontroller.
Connect the other end of the USB cable to the USB port of a laptop.
Download and install the Arduino Desktop IDE.
Start the Arduino IDE, copying necessary code to the working directory of the IDE.
Upload and install the code to the microcontroller.
Cut, strip and solder a small spade terminal onto each wire (J in Fig 4, S6).
Drill and tap two holes in the polycarbonate sheet (K in Fig 4, S6) to mount the piezoelectric actuator (L in Fig 4, S6).
Insert the screw through one of the holes on the piezoelectric mount, the washers and spade terminals to attach the actuator to the polycarbonate sheet.
Repeat for the second screw to securely mount the actuator to the sheet.
Solder the wiring from the mounted actuator to the respective electrical spade terminals (red to red; black to black) connecting the piezoelectric to the control circuit.

Confirm that the control circuit works by attaching the components together, plugging in the power supply to the wall outlet and connecting the electrical output from the control circuit to the piezoelectric actuator.
Observe the piezoelectric deflect when the pushbutton is activated.
Construct collars using the published design specifications or purchase and modify them as necessary.
Set the space between metal plates in the collars precisely to 125 µm for optimal fly head compression.
Use the appropriate number of washers so that the gap between the surface of the collar and the piezoelectric is 393±13 µm.
Ensure the gap between calibration and actual experiments remains consistent.
Calibrate the device with a gap of 67±13 µm between the piezoelectric and the fly head.
Set up the dTBI device under the Leica Z16 APO macroscope.
Place a collar underneath the piezoelectric and move the 45°-angled mirror up against the collar.
Adjust the brightness, zoom and focus to capture the reflection of the piezoelectric in the angled mirror.
Capture 3 replicate videos of the piezoelectric deflection events in 5V steps from 35V to 80V at a frame rate of at least 10 fps.
Analyze the videos in FIJI using the Manual Tracking plugin to track a single pixel on the corner of the piezoelectric.
Generate a graph between voltage and y-displacement to ensure that the piezoelectric responds linearly to the voltage.
Set up the dTBI device and angled mirror under the Leica Z16 APO macroscope as specified.
Collar 5 flies according to detailed instructions in the dTBI procedure.
Position the last collared fly underneath the piezoelectric.
Place the angled mirror against the collar and adjust brightness, zoom, and focus to capture the reflection of the piezoelectric and the fly head in the mirror.
Capture videos of the compression event in 5V steps from 35V till 80V, using a fresh fly for each recording.
Obtain 3-6 replicate videos for each voltage step using flies of the same genotype obtained from different bottles to control for natural variation in head size.
Analyze the videos in FIJI and obtain the % head compression by comparing fly head heights between frames of no compression and maximum compression.
Perform a survival analysis on sham, mild, moderate and severe injury to identify the median lifespan.
Assess the device every 6 months for piezoelectric wear and tear using 6 flies.
Measure the % head compression at the voltage calibrated for 45%.
Verify that the newly measured compression is not significantly different from the calculated value during calibration.
Replace the piezoelectric if the newly measured compression is lower than the calibrated compression.
Re-measure the % head compression for 45% after replacement to ensure comparability with the original measurement.
Use 7d post-injury survival to verify that the biological response of the new piezoelectric is similar to the old one.
Verify the gap between the head and piezoelectric is similar across all 6 flies before calibration.
Generate voltage vs. displacement and voltage vs. head compression graphs for each voltage setting using 3-6 replicates per setting.
Calculate the voltage required for 35% (mild), 40% (moderate) and 45% (severe) compression using linear regression analyses.
Perform a survival analysis on sham, mild, moderate, and severe injury groups to identify median lifespan.
Conduct a 7d post-injury survival assay on severe dTBI flies.
Determine the number of flies needed for the experiment considering dTBI severity, final experimental readout and aging timeframe.
Collect required number of flies in fresh food vials in groups of 30 or less, and age them to 3 days.
Briefly anesthetize a vial of 3-day-old flies using CO₂ pad.
Place collar on the CO₂ pad with opening on right side.
Select single fly under stereo microscope and pick it up by both wings using blunt-ended forceps.
Manipulate the fly onto its right side, ensuring both wings are grasped close to the body for better control.
Bring the fly to the opening of the collar and gently thread the neck through the gap between the metal plates.
Ensure the head is stably resting on the metal plates before proceeding further.
Flip the collar over and push the fly to the far end.
Hold the forceps closed and rest them vertically on the metal groove against the right side of the fly body.
Push against the fly body gently so that it moves smoothly along the collar.
Move the fly by sliding the forceps along the groove made by the metal plates rather than pushing directly against the body to avoid injury.
Use a paintbrush to nudge the head with short pushes as an alternative method to move the fly more safely.
Collar 5-6 flies per collar, starting with the dTBI group and then the sham group.
Grasp the collar firmly with the left hand and push down lightly.
Push down on top of the metal plates near the opening of the collar with the right hand.
Slide the collar underneath the piezoelectric while pushing down lightly with both hands.
Position the head so that the piezoelectric is above the third antennal segment under the stereo microscope.
Ensure the neighboring fly is far enough away to avoid damage from the piezoelectric as it deflects.
Push the button that deflects the piezoelectric with the right hand while holding the collar in place with the left hand.
Gently slide the collar out from under the piezoelectric.
Use forceps or a paintbrush to remove the injured fly onto a CO₂ pad.
Slide the next fly along the collar to the dTBI spot.
Repeat steps for all remaining flies.
Collect the cohort of dTBI flies into a fresh food vial.
Remove sham flies from the collar and collect them into a fresh food vial.
Repeat steps until the desired number of flies have been injured.
Return the vials to the incubator to allow recovery.
Position heads under piezoelectric, ensuring it strikes all heads above the third antennal segment.
